p.src: When Sanshirō awoke from his doze, the woman had somehow begun talking with the old man beside her. The old man was unmistakably a country fellow who had boarded two stations back. He had come dashing aboard just before the train departed, shouting in an oddly shrill voice, and when he suddenly stripped to the waist, his back proved to be covered with moxibustion scars; that was why Sanshirō remembered him. Indeed, Sanshirō had watched him closely as he wiped away his sweat, put his clothes back on, and sat down beside the woman. Sanshirō and the woman had shared the carriage since Kyoto. She had caught Sanshirō's eye from the moment she boarded. For one thing, her complexion was dark. Since transferring from Kyushu to the Sanyō Line and drawing ever closer to Kyoto and Osaka, Sanshirō had watched women's complexions grow steadily fairer, and without realizing it he had felt the sadness of leaving his native country farther and farther behind. So when this woman entered the carriage, he somehow felt that he had gained an ally among the opposite sex. Her complexion was truly the complexion of Kyushu. It was the same shade as Omitsu of Miwada. Until just before he left home, Omitsu had seemed an annoying woman. He had been immensely grateful to get away from her. Yet viewed from here, someone like Omitsu did not seem at all bad. In looks alone, however, this woman was far superior. Her mouth was firm. Her eyes were clear and distinct. Her forehead was not broad and sprawling like Omitsu's. Somehow, all her features came together most pleasingly. And so Sanshirō raised his eyes to look at her about once every five minutes. At times, her eyes met his. When the old man sat down beside her, Sanshirō watched her especially closely, keeping his eyes on her for as long as he possibly could. At that moment the woman smiled, said, “Please, sit down,” and made room for the old man. A little while later, Sanshirō grew sleepy and fell asleep.

p.src: It seemed that while he slept, the woman and the old man had grown friendly and begun to talk. Sanshirō opened his eyes and silently listened to their conversation. The woman said the following: —When it comes to children's toys, Kyoto still has better ones at lower prices than Hiroshima. She had briefly got off in Kyoto on an errand and, while there, bought some toys near Takoyakushi. She was happy to be returning home and seeing her child after so long. But she was worried because her husband's remittances had stopped, leaving her no choice but to return to her parents' home. Her husband had long worked as a civilian laborer for the navy in Kure, but during the war he had gone to Port Arthur. After the war ended, he returned once. Before long, saying there was more money to be made over there, he went off again to work in Dalian. At first all was well: he kept in touch and unfailingly sent money every month. But about six months ago, both his letters and the money stopped coming altogether. He was not an unfaithful sort, so she was sure he would be all right; but she could not go on living in idleness forever, and until she learned whether he was safe, she had no choice but to return to her parents' home and wait there.

p.src: The old man seemed neither to know of Takoyakushi nor to have any interest in toys, and at first he merely answered yes, yes; but when the story reached Port Arthur, he suddenly grew sympathetic and declared that it was truly a great pity. His own son, too, had been taken into the army during the war and had finally died over there. He could not understand what wars were fought for in the first place. It might be different if prosperity followed, but precious sons were killed and prices rose. Nothing could be more absurd. In better times, there had been no such thing as leaving home to find work. It was all thanks to the war. In any case, faith was what mattered most. He must surely be alive and working somewhere. If she waited a little longer, he would surely come home. —Saying such things, the old man earnestly tried to console the woman. Before long the train stopped, and after bidding the woman farewell and telling her to take care, he strode cheerfully out. About four others got off after the old man, while only one new passenger boarded in their place. The carriage had not been crowded to begin with, and now it suddenly felt desolate. Perhaps it was because night had fallen. A railwayman tramped heavily across the roof, inserting lighted lamps from above as he went. As though suddenly remembering it, Sanshirō began eating the boxed meal he had bought at the previous station. About two minutes after the train had started moving, the same woman rose smoothly, passed Sanshirō, and went out of the compartment. It was then that the color of her sash first caught Sanshirō's eye. With the head of a simmered sweetfish still between his teeth, Sanshirō watched her receding figure. Thinking she must have gone to the lavatory, he went on eating steadily. Presently the woman returned. This time he saw her from the front. Sanshirō was nearly finished with his meal. Looking down, he vigorously worked his chopsticks and crammed in another two or three mouthfuls, but the woman still did not seem to be returning to her former seat.

p.src: Wondering if that might be so, he glanced up and found her standing directly in front of him after all. But the instant Sanshirō raised his eyes, the woman began to move. Instead of simply passing Sanshirō and returning to her seat, she came straight forward, turned sideways, put her head out of the window, and began quietly gazing outside. The wind struck her hard, and Sanshirō saw the hair at her temples fluttering. At that moment Sanshirō flung the empty meal box out of the window with all his strength. The woman's window and Sanshirō's were separated by one window. When the lid he had thrown against the wind seemed to flutter whitely back, Sanshirō realized he might have done something dreadful and glanced at the woman's face. Unfortunately, her face was outside the train. But the woman quietly drew her head back in and began carefully wiping her forehead with a printed cotton handkerchief. Sanshirō decided that, at any rate, apologizing would be the safest course.

p.src: “I’m sorry,” he said. “Not at all,” the woman replied. She was still wiping her face. Sanshirō had no choice but to fall silent. The woman fell silent too. Then she put her head out of the window again. The three or four other passengers all wore drowsy expressions beneath the dim lamp. No one was speaking. Only the train thundered onward with a tremendous roar. Sanshirō closed his eyes. After a while, he heard the woman ask, “Will we be in Nagoya soon?” When he looked, he saw that she had turned around without his noticing and was leaning toward him, her face brought close to his. Sanshirō was startled. “I suppose so,” he said, but since this was his first journey to Tokyo, he had no real idea. “Do you think we’ll be late at this rate?” “I expect so.” “Are you getting off at Nagoya too...?” “Yes, I am.” The train terminated at Nagoya. The conversation was exceedingly ordinary. The only change was that the woman now sat diagonally opposite Sanshirō. And so, for a while, there was once again nothing but the sound of the train. When the train stopped at the next station, the woman finally asked Sanshirō if, inconvenient though it might be, he would guide her to an inn when they reached Nagoya. She pleaded repeatedly, saying that being alone made her uneasy. Sanshirō thought her request reasonable enough. Yet he did not feel inclined to accept it gladly. After all, she was a woman he did not know, so he hesitated considerably; but lacking the courage to refuse her outright, he gave her a vague, noncommittal answer. Before long, the train arrived in Nagoya. His large wicker trunk had been checked through to Shimbashi, so he had no need to worry about it. Carrying only a handy canvas bag and an umbrella, Sanshirō left through the ticket gate. On his head he wore his high-school summer cap. But as a sign that he had graduated, he had torn off the badge.

p.src: The train due at nine-thirty had arrived about forty minutes late, so it was already past ten. But because it was the hot season, the town was still as lively as if the evening had only just begun. There were two or three inns directly in front of them. They merely seemed a little too grand for Sanshirō. So he walked calmly past the electrically lit three-story buildings and wandered on. Naturally, since he did not know the place, he had no idea where he was heading. He simply went in the darker direction. The woman followed without saying a word. Then, on the second building from the corner of a relatively quiet side street, he saw a sign reading “Lodgings.” It was a suitably shabby sign for both Sanshirō and the woman. Sanshirō glanced back and briefly asked the woman what she thought; when she said it would do, he made up his mind and went straight in. At the entrance, Sanshirō should have explained that they were not traveling together, but the staff rattled on—“Welcome! Do come in! This way, please! Plum Room Number Four!”—so, unable to intervene, they were both silently shown to Plum Room Number Four. While the maid brought tea, the two sat facing each other in a daze. When the maid brought the tea and suggested a bath, Sanshirō no longer had enough courage to explain that the woman was not his companion. So, with a towel dangling from his hand, he said, “I’ll go first,” and left for the bathroom. The bathroom was at the end of the corridor, next to the lavatory. It was dim and appeared quite filthy. Sanshirō took off his clothes, climbed into the bath, and thought for a moment. As he splashed about, thinking what a troublesome business this was, he heard footsteps in the corridor. Someone seemed to have gone into the lavatory. Presently, the person came out. The person washed their hands. When that was done, the bathroom door creaked halfway open. The same woman stood at the entrance and asked, “Shall I scrub your back a little?”

p.src: Sanshirō declined in a loud voice, saying, “No, thank you. I’ve had enough.” But the woman did not go out. Instead, she came farther in. Then she began to undo her sash. It seemed that she meant to bathe with Sanshirō. Nor did she appear particularly embarrassed. Sanshirō sprang out of the bath at once. He hastily dried himself, returned to the room, and sat down on a cushion, still considerably shaken, when the maid brought in the guest register.

p.src: Sanshirō took up the register and honestly wrote, “Ogawa Sanshirō, Masaki Village, Miyako District, Fukuoka Prefecture; age twenty-three; student,” but when he came to the woman’s entry, he was completely at a loss. He thought he should have waited until she came out of the bath, but it was too late now. The maid stood waiting attentively beside him. With no other choice, he invented an entry—“Hana, same surname, village, district, and prefecture; age twenty-three”—and handed the register back. Then he kept fanning himself vigorously. Before long, the woman returned. “I’m terribly sorry for my rudeness,” she said. “Not at all,” Sanshirō replied. Sanshirō took a notebook from his bag and began writing his diary. There was nothing at all to write. He felt that if the woman were not there, he would have plenty to write about. Then the woman said, “I’m just stepping out for a moment,” and left the room. Now Sanshirō found it even harder to write his diary. He began wondering where she had gone. Just then, the maid came in to lay out the bedding. She had brought only one broad futon, and when he told her that two beds must be laid out, she made excuses about the room being too small and the mosquito net too narrow, and they got nowhere. She also seemed to find the whole business bothersome. At last she said, “The clerk has just stepped out. When he returns, I’ll ask him and bring another one,” then stubbornly spread the single futon across the full width of the mosquito net and left. A little while later, the woman returned. “I’m terribly sorry to be so late,” she said. While she was doing something in the shadow of the mosquito net, there came a clattering sound. It must have been the toy she was taking home as a present for her child. Presently, she seemed to have tied the cloth-wrapped bundle back up as before. From beyond the mosquito net came her voice: “I’ll turn in first, then.” Sanshirō merely answered, “Ah,” and remained sitting on the threshold, fanning himself. He even considered spending the whole night just as he was. But the mosquitoes came buzzing around him.

p.src: He could never endure the whole night outside the net. Sanshirō rose abruptly, took a calico shirt and a pair of drawers from his bag, put them on over his bare skin, and tied a dark-blue soft sash around them. Then, carrying two Western-style towels, he went inside the mosquito net. In the far corner beyond the futon, the woman was still moving her fan.

p.src: “Excuse me, but I’m rather fastidious and dislike sleeping in someone else’s bedding... Please forgive me while I devise a little protection against the fleas.” Saying this, Sanshirō began rolling the spare edge of the sheet toward the side where the woman lay. In this way he made a long white partition down the middle of the bedding. The woman rolled over to face the other way. Sanshirō spread out two Western-style towels lengthwise across his allotted territory and lay stretched out narrowly upon them. That night, neither Sanshirō’s hands nor his feet strayed even an inch beyond the narrow width of those towels. The woman did not say a word. She, too, remained perfectly still, facing the wall. At long last, dawn came. After they had washed their faces and sat down to breakfast, the woman smiled and asked, “Were there any fleas last night?” Looking down, Sanshirō solemnly replied with something like, “No, thank you; thanks to you,” while busily prodding the simmered beans in a sake cup. After they had paid the bill, left the inn, and reached the station, the woman told Sanshirō for the first time that she was taking the Kansai Line toward Yokkaichi. Sanshirō’s train soon arrived. Because of the timetable, the woman had a little longer to wait. Having accompanied him as far as the ticket gate, the woman bowed politely. “Thank you for all your help... Well, take care.” Still holding his bag and umbrella in one hand, Sanshirō removed his familiar old hat with the other and said only, “Goodbye.” The woman gazed steadily at his face, then said in a composed tone, “You really are a very timid man,” and gave him a sly smile. Sanshirō felt as though he had been flung out onto the platform. Once inside the carriage, both his ears burned hotter still.

p.src: When the man looked at him, Sanshirō felt vaguely embarrassed. Thinking he might distract himself with a book, he opened his bag and found the Western-style towels from the previous night packed tightly across the top. He raked them aside and pulled out the first thing his hand touched at the bottom. It was a collection of Bacon’s essays that he could not understand even if he read it. It was such a thin, shabbily paper-bound volume that one almost felt sorry for Bacon. He had never intended to read it on the train, but it had failed to find its way into the large wicker trunk, so while tidying up he had tossed it into the bottom of his traveling bag with two or three other books. By ill luck, it was the one he had now drawn. Sanshirō opened Bacon to page twenty-three. He did not feel capable of reading any other book either. Still less, of course, did he feel like reading Bacon. Nevertheless, Sanshirō reverently held page twenty-three open and let his gaze travel evenly over the whole page. Before page twenty-three, Sanshirō intended to review the events of the previous night. What sort of woman was she, after all? Could there really be such a woman in the world? Could women truly remain so composed and unconcerned? Was she uneducated, or was she bold? Or was she simply innocent? In the end, since he had not gone as far as things might have gone, he had no way of knowing. He wished he had summoned his courage and gone a little further. But it was frightening. When she told him at parting that he was a timid man, he had been astonished. It felt as though the weakness of all his twenty-three years had been exposed at once. Not even his own parents could have struck the mark so neatly. —At this point in his reflections, Sanshirō grew more dejected still. He felt as though some nobody of unknown origin had given him such a dressing-down that he could never hold up his head before her again.

p.src: It would never do to lose his head like that. What good were learning and being a university student then? It reflected very badly on his character. Surely he could have handled it a little better. Yet if the other party always acted that way, it seemed to him that, as an educated man, he could hardly have responded otherwise. That would mean he must never approach women recklessly. It seemed rather spineless. It was terribly constraining. It was almost as though he had been born disabled. But then... Sanshirō abruptly changed the course of his thoughts and recalled another world. —Now he was going to Tokyo. He would enter the university. He would meet famous scholars. He would associate with students of taste and character. He would conduct research in the library. He would write books. The world would applaud him. His mother would be delighted. As he idly indulged in visions of such a future and recovered all his spirits, he no longer felt any need to keep his face buried in page twenty-three. So he suddenly raised his head. The man from before, seated diagonally opposite, was looking at Sanshirō again. This time Sanshirō looked back at him. He had a thick beard. He was a lean man with a long face and something vaguely Shinto-priestly about him. Only his straight, well-defined nose looked Western. Still in the course of his formal education, Sanshirō invariably took a man like this for a teacher. Beneath a white kasuri kimono, the man had carefully layered a white under-robe, and he wore navy tabi socks. Judging from this attire, Sanshirō identified him as a middle-school teacher. To one such as himself, with a great future ahead, the man somehow seemed insignificant. The man must already have been forty. He did not look likely to advance any further in life. The man kept puffing away at his cigarette. When he blew long streams of smoke from his nostrils and folded his arms, he looked remarkably unhurried.

p.src: Yet at other times he would get up incessantly, apparently to go to the lavatory or somewhere. Sometimes, as he rose, he would stretch with all his might. He looked thoroughly bored. When the passenger beside him set down a newspaper he had finished, the man showed no inclination even to borrow it. Sanshirō naturally began to feel awkward and laid Bacon's essays facedown. He considered taking out a novel and making a serious attempt to read it, but decided that would be too much trouble. Instead, he found himself wanting to borrow the newspaper belonging to the man in front of him. Unfortunately, the man in front was snoring soundly. Reaching out and placing a hand on the newspaper, Sanshirō deliberately asked the bearded man, “Are you finished with it?” With an unconcerned expression, the man said, “I should think it's free. Go ahead and read it.” Having picked up the newspaper, Sanshirō was the one who now felt ill at ease.

p.src: When he opened it, he found nothing in the newspaper particularly worth reading. He finished reading it through in a minute or two. As he conscientiously folded it and returned it to its former place, he gave a slight bow; the man opposite returned the greeting and asked, “Are you a higher-school student?” Sanshirō was pleased that the man had noticed the mark left by the badge on the old cap he was wearing. “Yes,” he replied. “In Tokyo?” Only when the man asked him back did he say, “No, Kumamoto. ...But...” Then he fell silent. He had wanted to say that he was a university student, but held back, thinking there was no particular need to mention it. The other man merely said, “Ah, I see,” and went on smoking. He did not ask why a student from Kumamoto was going to Tokyo at this time of year, or anything else. Apparently, students from Kumamoto did not interest him. At that moment, the man sleeping in front of Sanshirō said, “Mm, I see.” Yet he was unmistakably asleep. Nor was he merely talking in his sleep. The bearded man looked at Sanshirō and grinned. Taking the opportunity, Sanshirō asked, “And where are you going?” “Tokyo,” the man said slowly, and nothing more. Somehow, he was beginning to seem less like a middle-school teacher. Still, since he was traveling third class, it was clear that he was no person of great consequence. With that, Sanshirō brought the conversation to an end. The bearded man remained with his arms folded, occasionally beating time with the front teeth of his wooden clogs and tapping the floor. He looked thoroughly bored. But his was the sort of boredom that had no desire for conversation. When the train reached Toyohashi, the sleeping man abruptly sat up, rubbed his eyes, and got off. Sanshirō wondered how anyone could manage to wake at precisely the right moment.

p.src: Watching through the window, Sanshirō worried that perhaps the man was still half asleep and had mistaken the station, but that was plainly not the case. He passed safely through the ticket gate and walked out like a man in full possession of his senses. Relieved, Sanshirō moved to the seat opposite. This put him beside the bearded man. The bearded man, taking his turn, leaned his head out of the window to buy honey peaches.

p.src: Presently he placed the fruit between them and said, “Would you like one?” Sanshirō thanked him and ate one. The bearded man evidently liked them, for he ate one after another with abandon. He urged Sanshirō to have more. Sanshirō ate another. While the two of them ate the peaches, they grew considerably more familiar and began talking about all sorts of things. According to the man, the peach was the most immortal-like of all fruits. Its flavor was somehow rather foolish. To begin with, the stone was clumsily shaped. What was more, it was riddled with holes and fashioned in a most curious way, he said. Sanshirō had never heard this theory before, but thought the man was talking a great deal of nonsense. Then the man began telling him this. Shiki was extremely fond of fruit. And he was a man who could eat any quantity of it. Once he ate sixteen large barrel-ripened persimmons. And suffered no ill effects at all. Someone like me could never imitate Shiki. —Sanshirō listened with a smile. Yet he felt that the part about Shiki alone held some interest for him. Just as he was thinking of saying a little more about Shiki, the man continued, “When people like something, their hands naturally reach for it, you know. It cannot be helped. Pigs cannot reach out their hands, so they reach out their snouts instead. They say that if you tie up a pig so it cannot move and set a feast just before its snout, then, because it cannot move, the tip of its snout gradually grows longer. They say it keeps growing until it reaches the food. Nothing is so frightening as single-minded desire,” he said, grinning. His manner of speaking made it difficult to tell clearly whether he was serious or joking. “Well, we should both be grateful we are not pigs. If our noses stretched recklessly toward everything we wanted, by now they would surely be so long that we could not even board a train, and that would be troublesome.” Sanshirō burst out laughing.

p.src: “It really is dangerous. A man named Leonardo da Vinci once injected arsenic into the trunk of a peach tree to test whether the poison would spread into its fruit. And someone ate one of those peaches and died. Dangerous. You have to be careful—it’s dangerous,” he said, gathering the pits and skins of the honey peaches he had devoured and scattered about, wrapping them all together in newspaper, and tossing the bundle out the window. This time Sanshirō did not feel like laughing. The name Leonardo da Vinci had already rather daunted him; then, for some reason, he began thinking about the woman from the previous night and grew strangely ill at ease, so he discreetly fell silent. His companion, however, seemed entirely unaware of any of this. Presently he asked, “Where are you going in Tokyo?” “Actually, it’s my first time there, so I don’t really know my way around… For the time being, I think I may go to my province’s dormitory,” Sanshirō replied. “Then you’re finished with Kumamoto…?” “I graduated this time.” “Ah, is that so,” the man said, without adding either congratulations or how splendid. He merely asked, as though it were the most commonplace thing in the world, “So now you’ll be entering the university?” Sanshirō felt somewhat disappointed. In return, he disposed of the exchange with a simple “Yes.” “What division?” the man asked again. “The First Division.” “Law?” “No, literature.” “Ah, is that so,” he said again. Each time Sanshirō heard that “Ah, is that so,” it left him with a peculiar feeling. Either the man was extremely eminent, or he treated others with utter contempt; otherwise, he had to be someone wholly without ties to or sympathy for the university. But since Sanshirō could not tell which of these was the case, his own manner toward the man remained extremely uncertain. At Hamamatsu, the two of them ate their boxed lunches as if by prior agreement.

p.src: Even after they had finished eating, the train showed no sign of leaving. Looking out the window, Sanshirō saw four or five Westerners pacing back and forth in front of the train. One pair among them appeared to be husband and wife, and despite the heat they were walking arm in arm. The woman was dressed entirely in white and was exceedingly beautiful. In all his life up to that day, Sanshirō had seen only five or six Westerners. Two of them were teachers at the higher school in Kumamoto, and one of those two had unfortunately been a hunchback. The only Western woman he knew was a missionary. Her face was extraordinarily pointed, resembling a whiting or a ※. So a splendid, beautiful Westerner like this was more than merely a rarity to him. She appeared to him a truly superior being. Sanshirō gazed at her in utter fascination. He thought it only natural that people like these should act superior. He even imagined how painfully insignificant he would feel if he went to the West and found himself among such people. When the couple passed the window, he listened intently to their conversation, but could not understand a word. Their pronunciation seemed entirely different from that of his teachers in Kumamoto.

p.src: Just then, the same man poked his head out from behind and said, “It doesn’t look as though it will appear yet, does it?” He glanced at the Western couple who had just passed by, murmured, “Ah, beautiful,” and immediately gave a halfhearted yawn. Sanshirō realized how thoroughly rustic he must look, promptly drew his head back in, and sat down. The man followed him back to his seat. Then he said, “Westerners really are beautiful, aren’t they?” Sanshirō could think of no particular reply, so he merely said, “Indeed,” and smiled. Then the bearded man began, “We are a sorry lot, you and I.” “With faces like these, and as feeble as we are, it is no use winning the Russo-Japanese War and becoming a first-rate power. To be sure, our buildings and gardens are much what one would expect from faces like ours—but if this is your first time in Tokyo, you cannot have seen Mount Fuji yet. It will come into view soon, so have a look. That is Japan’s foremost attraction. We have nothing else to boast of. But Mount Fuji has simply stood there by nature since ancient times, so there is nothing to be done about that. We did not make it,” he said, grinning again. Sanshirō had never imagined that, after the Russo-Japanese War, he would encounter a man like this. Somehow, the man did not seem Japanese. “But surely Japan will continue to develop from now on,” he said in its defense. The man, entirely unperturbed, replied, “It will perish.” —If anyone said such a thing aloud in Kumamoto, he would be struck at once. At worst, he would be branded a traitor. Sanshirō had grown up in an atmosphere that left not the smallest corner of his mind free to admit an idea like this. He therefore wondered whether the man might be taking advantage of his youth to make a fool of him. The man was grinning as usual.

p.src: “Tokyo is larger than Kumamoto. Japan is larger than Tokyo. Japan is smaller than…” He paused there for a moment, but when he looked at Sanshirō, he saw him listening intently. “Your mind is larger than Japan, wouldn’t you say?” he continued. “You must not let yourself be constrained. However much you care for Japan, blind partiality will only end up doing it harm.” When Sanshirō heard these words, he felt that he had truly left Kumamoto behind. At the same time, he realized how very cowardly he had been while living there. That evening, Sanshirō arrived in Tokyo. The bearded man did not reveal his name even when they parted. Sanshirō believed that once he reached Tokyo, men of this sort would be found everywhere, so he made no particular attempt to ask the man’s name.
